title: Causes and characteristics

blocks.heading: Causes and characteristics
blocks.text: Rural–urban migration, different rates of natural population change and changes in settlement classification can affect the urban share. People may move in response to rural constraints and perceived urban opportunities, but migration and urbanisation are not interchangeable concepts. A push factor encourages departure, such as loss of a livelihood; a pull factor attracts people, such as access to work or education. A perceived opportunity may not become an actual job. Births and deaths in urban and rural populations also affect their relative sizes. Changing a boundary can alter measured shares without people physically moving, so compare definitions before drawing conclusions.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Industrialised-country patterns
blocks.text: Many industrialised economies experienced substantial earlier rural–urban movement associated with industrial employment and service concentration. Where a large share is already urban, further growth, suburban movement or movement away from city centres can follow different patterns. These are broad historical tendencies, not current country rankings or rules for every resident. Movement from one urban area to another can change a city’s population without changing the national urban share. A crowded city alone does not show how quickly a country is urbanising. Use the supplied dates and denominators.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Developing-country patterns
blocks.text: Some developing economies experience rapid urban growth where migration and natural increase combine with a growing urban share. If housing, services and work opportunities expand more slowly than needs, existing access gaps can widen. The rate and form vary between countries and settlements. Urban residents can benefit from concentrated markets, schools and services; rapid growth creates pressure when provision cannot keep pace. Avoid describing urban growth as an automatic cause of poverty or assuming that all residents have the same experience.

blocks.heading: Read a pattern rather than assume one
blocks.text: In an original fictional comparison, Area A’s urban share rises from 30% to 45%, with an annual net rural–urban inflow of 5,000; Area B’s share rises from 70% to 72%, with an inflow of 500. Both urbanise, but A has the larger percentage-point rise and supplied inflow. These observations support a contrast, not proof that migration caused the whole change. The periods and definitions must match. Topic 7.1 develops natural change and migration; do not confuse a higher starting level with faster urbanisation.

blocks.heading: Connect causes and responses
blocks.text: Industrialisation in Topic 4.1 explains some work opportunities. Rural development in Topic 5.1 explains opportunities at origins. Neither turns all migration into one simple cause.
